blocks.text: ECONOMICS
SEMESTER I & II
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

Rural development means the overall improvement of the economic and social conditions of people living in rural areas. It includes higher income and employment, better infrastructure, reduction of poverty and improved access to education, health and other basic services.

Rural development is a multi-dimensional process. It is not limited to increasing agricultural output; it also covers better nutrition, literacy, health, housing, drinking water, sanitation, social justice and the empowerment of weaker sections such as women, landless labourers, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

In simple words, rural development aims to make villages good places to live and work. It seeks to raise the productivity and income of rural people, create opportunities outside farming, strengthen local institutions such as panchayats and co-operatives, and reduce the gap between rural and urban living standards.

The basic elements of rural development include improvement in living standards, employment and productive opportunities, access to essential services, participation of rural people and reduction of poverty and inequality.

Three core values are often used to explain these elements: (1) life-sustenance, meaning the ability to meet basic needs such as food, shelter, health and protection; (2) self-esteem, meaning a sense of worth and dignity; and (3) freedom, meaning a wider range of choices for individuals and communities.

In practice the elements include agricultural growth, development of rural industries, infrastructure such as roads, power and irrigation, human resource development through education and health, social justice through land reforms and welfare schemes, and people's participation through Panchayati Raj institutions.

sections.title: Need and Importance of Rural Development

blocks.text: Rural development is important because a large section of India's population depends directly or indirectly on the rural economy. It helps reduce poverty and unemployment, raise agricultural productivity, develop infrastructure and reduce excessive pressure on urban areas.

Nearly two-thirds of India's population lives in villages, and agriculture and allied activities still employ a large share of the workforce. Unless rural incomes rise, national poverty, malnutrition and unemployment cannot be removed.

Rural development also strengthens the whole economy. Higher rural income creates demand for industrial goods, agriculture supplies food and raw materials, and better rural facilities slow down distress migration to cities, which otherwise leads to slums and overcrowding. It also promotes social equality, political stability and balanced regional development.

The rural economy includes agriculture and non-agricultural activities. Agriculture remains important for employment and livelihood, while non-farm activities such as small industries, trade, transport and services provide additional sources of income.

Important features of the rural economy include heavy dependence on agriculture, a high share of small and marginal farmers, seasonal and disguised unemployment, low levels of capital, limited infrastructure and a large informal sector.

Over time the rural economy has been diversifying. Dairying, poultry, fisheries, horticulture, handicrafts, food processing, construction and rural services have grown, and remittances from migrant workers also support rural households. This diversification makes rural incomes more stable.

Major problems include low productivity, small holdings, inadequate irrigation and infrastructure, limited access to credit, marketing difficulties, dependence on weather and unequal access to technology and resources.

Low productivity arises because of small and fragmented holdings, traditional methods, poor quality seeds and limited use of modern inputs. Nearly half of the cropped area depends on rainfall, so failure or uneven distribution of the monsoon causes crop loss.

Farmers also face lack of storage, cold chains and transport, the presence of middlemen, price fluctuations, high costs of inputs and indebtedness. Soil degradation, falling groundwater levels and climate change add to these problems. Solutions include irrigation expansion, land consolidation, better credit and marketing, crop insurance, research and extension services.

The rural non-agricultural sector includes manufacturing, construction, trade, transport and services. It creates employment outside farming, diversifies rural income and reduces excessive dependence on agriculture.

The rural non-farm sector (RNFS) covers activities such as agro-processing, handloom and handicrafts, khadi and village industries, small workshops, shops, transport services, construction and repair work.

Its importance lies in absorbing surplus labour from agriculture, providing employment during the off-season, raising household income, using local raw materials and skills, and reducing migration to cities. It also helps women and landless households who have little or no land to cultivate.
The syllabus identifies natural resources, human resources, capital and technology as major determinants. Their quantity, quality and effective use influence rural productivity and development.

Natural resources such as land, water, forests and minerals form the base of rural production. Human resources matter because a healthy, educated and skilled population can adopt better techniques. Capital, both physical (tools, machinery, irrigation works) and financial (credit), is needed for investment, while technology such as improved seeds, fertilizers and machines raises productivity.

Besides these, institutional factors such as land tenure, credit institutions, co-operatives and panchayats, and government policy also determine the pace of rural development. The best results come when all these determinants are improved together.

Rural infrastructure includes roads, transport, electricity, irrigation, communication, schools, health facilities, markets and financial services. Good infrastructure increases productivity and improves access to opportunities and services.

Rural infrastructure may be divided into economic infrastructure (roads, power, irrigation, telecommunications, markets, banks) and social infrastructure (schools, hospitals, drinking water, sanitation, housing).

Good infrastructure reduces transport costs, connects farmers to markets, allows the use of modern inputs and machinery, attracts industries to rural areas and improves the quality of life. Programmes such as PMGSY for rural roads, rural electrification and the Jal Jeevan Mission for tap water show the importance given to rural infrastructure in India.

Self-Help Groups are small voluntary groups whose members regularly save and often obtain credit collectively. SHGs promote savings, access to finance, mutual support and income-generating activities.

An SHG usually has 10 to 20 members, often women from similar economic backgrounds. Members save small amounts regularly, lend to one another from the common fund and, after a period of good functioning, are linked to banks for larger loans through the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme started by NABARD in 1992.

SHGs reduce dependence on moneylenders, encourage thrift, build confidence and leadership among women, and support small businesses such as weaving, tailoring, food processing and animal husbandry. Group responsibility (peer pressure) helps in good repayment of loans.

A co-operative society is a voluntary organization formed to serve the common economic interests of members. Co-operatives can provide credit, marketing, inputs and other services on the basis of mutual assistance.

Co-operatives work on principles such as voluntary and open membership, democratic control (one member, one vote), member economic participation, autonomy, education of members and concern for the community.

In rural India there are credit co-operatives (Primary Agricultural Credit Societies), marketing co-operatives, dairy co-operatives such as Amul, consumer co-operatives and processing co-operatives. They help small producers get better prices, cheaper inputs and credit. Their weaknesses include political interference, poor management and dominance of richer members.
Rural credit means loans and financial assistance provided for agricultural and other rural activities. It may be short-term, medium-term or long-term according to purpose and repayment period.

Short-term credit (up to 15 months) is needed for seeds, fertilizers, pesticides and wages. Medium-term credit (15 months to 5 years) is used for buying cattle, pump sets and small machinery. Long-term credit (more than 5 years) is needed for buying land, permanent land improvement, digging wells and costly machinery like tractors.

Credit may also be classified by purpose into productive credit (for production) and unproductive or consumption credit (for social ceremonies, illness and household needs). Adequate, timely and cheap credit is essential for raising agricultural productivity.
Institutional sources include NABARD, commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks and Cooperative Credit Societies. They provide organized credit under formal rules and regulations.

NABARD, established in 1982, is the apex institution that refinances banks for rural lending. Commercial banks expanded rural lending after nationalisation in 1969 and through priority-sector lending rules. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), set up from 1975, combine the local touch of co-operatives with the business skills of commercial banks. Co-operative credit societies form a three-tier structure: State Co-operative Banks, District Central Co-operative Banks and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies.
Institutional credit is cheaper, regulated and linked with development goals. The aim of policy has been to replace exploitative informal credit by institutional credit.
Non-institutional sources include moneylenders and other informal agencies. They may be easily accessible but can involve high interest rates and unfavourable terms.
Non-institutional sources include professional moneylenders, landlords, traders and commission agents, relatives and friends. Historically they supplied most rural credit.

Their advantages are easy availability, little paperwork and flexibility. However, they often charge very high interest, manipulate accounts, take land as security and may force borrowers to sell crops to them at low prices. This led to the cycle of indebtedness in rural India.
Problems include inadequate access to formal credit, lack of collateral, delays, indebtedness, dependence on informal lenders and difficulty in reaching small and marginal borrowers.

Small and marginal farmers often lack land titles, which makes it hard to offer security. Bank branches may be far away, procedures are complex and loans may come late in the season. Many loans are used for consumption, and crop failure leads to default.

Other problems include regional imbalance in credit supply, high overdues in co-operatives, political loan waivers that affect credit discipline, and continued dependence on moneylenders. Remedies include simplified procedures, Kisan Credit Cards, SHG linkage, crop insurance, financial literacy and digital banking.
Kisan Credit Card is a credit facility designed to provide farmers with convenient and timely access to credit for agricultural and related requirements.

The Kisan Credit Card scheme was introduced in 1998 on the recommendation of the R.V. Gupta Committee and is implemented by commercial banks, RRBs and co-operative banks. It gives a revolving credit limit to farmers based on their land holding and cropping pattern.

Farmers can withdraw money when needed for cultivation, post-harvest expenses and allied activities like animal husbandry and fisheries. Benefits include less paperwork, flexibility, interest subvention for prompt repayment, and insurance cover. It reduces dependence on moneylenders.

The Lewis model explains development through transfer of labour from a traditional subsistence sector to a modern capitalist sector. Expansion of the modern sector is supported by reinvestment of profits and absorption of surplus labour.

W. Arthur Lewis presented this model in 1954 ('Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour'). The traditional sector has surplus labour whose marginal productivity is near zero. The modern sector can therefore get labour at a constant subsistence wage, earn profits, reinvest them and keep expanding until surplus labour is exhausted (the Lewis turning point).

The model is useful for understanding structural transformation, but it has been criticised because modern industry may use labour-saving technology, urban wages may rise above subsistence, and there may be urban unemployment even while rural surplus labour exists.
The Gandhian model emphasizes self-reliant villages, local production, decentralized development, small and cottage industries, dignity of labour and improvement of rural life.

Gandhi believed that 'India lives in her villages'. His model aimed at Gram Swaraj, where each village is self-sufficient in basic needs such as food, clothing and shelter. He emphasised khadi and village industries, use of local resources, decentralised decision-making through village panchayats and trusteeship in place of exploitation.

The model also stressed non-violence, simple living, removal of untouchability, basic education (Nai Talim) and production by the masses rather than mass production. Many ideas such as Panchayati Raj, KVIC and the promotion of cottage industries reflect Gandhian thinking.
Rural development policies are government measures designed to improve rural livelihoods, employment, housing, infrastructure and productive capacity.

Since independence India has followed several approaches: the Community Development Programme (1952), the Green Revolution strategy, target-group programmes such as SFDA and IRDP, wage employment schemes, and later rights-based and livelihood approaches.

Present policies focus on employment (MGNREGA), housing (PMAY-G), livelihoods (DAY-NRLM), rural roads (PMGSY), drinking water (Jal Jeevan Mission), sanitation (Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen), farmer income support (PM-KISAN) and decentralised planning through panchayats.
MGNREGA provides a legal framework for guaranteed wage employment to rural households through public works. It seeks livelihood security and creation of useful rural assets.

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in 2005 and implemented from 2006. It guarantees at least 100 days of unskilled manual wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to work.

Key features include work within 5 km of residence, payment of wages within 15 days, unemployment allowance if work is not given within 15 days, at least one-third participation of women, social audits, and works such as water conservation, land development and rural roads. It provides a safety net and reduces distress migration, though delays in wage payment remain a problem.
Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana aims to improve access to housing. In the rural context it supports eligible rural households in obtaining pucca housing with basic amenities.
PMAY-Gramin was launched in 2016 by restructuring the earlier Indira Awaas Yojana. Beneficiaries are selected using the Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) data and verified by Gram Sabhas.

Financial assistance is provided for constructing a pucca house (higher assistance in hilly and difficult areas such as the North-East, including Mizoram). The scheme converges with MGNREGA for unskilled labour, Swachh Bharat Mission for toilets, and other schemes for electricity, LPG and drinking water. Payments are made directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts.
The National Rural Livelihoods Mission promotes sustainable livelihoods, particularly through organization of rural poor into self-help groups, access to finance and livelihood support.

NRLM was launched in 2011 by restructuring the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana and was renamed Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-NRLM (DAY-NRLM) in 2016. It aims to bring at least one woman member from each poor rural household into SHGs and then federate them at village and block levels.

The mission provides revolving funds, community investment funds, bank linkage, skill training and support for farm and non-farm livelihoods. Its approach is 'by the poor, for the poor', building strong community institutions that help the poor come out of poverty.

sections.title: Concept, Elements, Need and Importance of Rural Development

blocks.text:
Rural development refers to the overall improvement of economic and social life in rural areas. It is broader than agricultural development because rural people depend on agriculture as well as non-farm occupations and public services.

Its basic elements include improvement in living standards, employment and productive opportunities, access to education, health and infrastructure, and greater participation of rural communities. Rural development is needed to reduce poverty and unemployment, improve productivity and create more balanced development between rural and urban areas.

India's rural economy contains both agricultural and non-agricultural sectors. Agriculture provides livelihood and raw materials but faces problems such as low productivity, infrastructure gaps, credit and marketing difficulties. The non-agricultural sector creates alternative employment and income. Rural development therefore requires simultaneous improvement of farming, non-farm activity, infrastructure and human capabilities.

Meaning in detail: The World Bank described rural development as a strategy designed to improve the economic and social life of a specific group of people, the rural poor. It therefore includes small farmers, tenants, landless labourers and artisans. It is a process of change in which rural communities move from a low standard of living to a better quality of life.

Elements: (1) Increase in agricultural and allied production; (2) creation of non-farm employment; (3) development of infrastructure such as roads, electricity, irrigation and communication; (4) provision of education, health, housing, water and sanitation; (5) social justice through land reforms and welfare of weaker sections; (6) people's participation through Panchayati Raj and community organisations; (7) environmental sustainability.

Need and importance: Most of India's poor live in villages. Rural development reduces poverty and unemployment, increases demand for industrial goods, ensures food security, checks rural-urban migration, reduces regional imbalance and strengthens democracy at the grassroots. It is also necessary for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

Problems of agriculture and the role of the non-farm sector: Agriculture faces small holdings, rainfall dependence, poor irrigation, soil degradation, credit and marketing problems and price instability. The non-farm sector - rural industries, trade, transport, construction and services - absorbs surplus labour, gives off-season work and diversifies income. A balanced strategy develops both sectors along with human capabilities. In conclusion, rural development is the foundation of national development in India.

Rural development depends upon natural resources, human resources, capital and technology. Natural resources provide the physical base for production. Human resources contribute labour, knowledge and skills. Capital supports investment, while technology can raise productivity and improve production methods.

Rural infrastructure includes roads, transport, electricity, irrigation, communication, schools, health facilities, markets and financial institutions. Poor infrastructure raises costs and restricts access to opportunities.

Self-Help Groups encourage small savings, collective credit and mutual support, while co-operative societies organize members around common economic needs such as credit, inputs and marketing. Both can strengthen participation and local economic organization.

Determinants explained: Natural resources set the limit of what can be produced; their conservation is necessary for sustainable growth. Human resources become productive through education, training and health care. Capital formation in rural areas is low because incomes and savings are low, so credit and public investment are important. Technology - improved seeds, fertilizers, irrigation methods, machinery and ICT - is the key to raising productivity. Institutions and governance also matter.

Role of infrastructure: Roads link villages to markets and services; electricity supports irrigation pumps and small industries; irrigation reduces dependence on the monsoon; communication and internet allow access to information and digital banking; markets and storage protect farmers from distress sales; schools and health centres build human capital. Lack of infrastructure keeps villages isolated and poor.

SHGs: They are small groups, mostly of women, that save regularly, lend internally and borrow from banks. They promote financial inclusion, women's empowerment, entrepreneurship and social awareness. NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme and DAY-NRLM have spread SHGs across India.

Co-operatives: Based on mutual help and democratic control, co-operatives provide credit, inputs, marketing, processing and storage. Successful examples include dairy co-operatives under Operation Flood. Their limitations are mismanagement, political interference and inadequate funds. Strengthening SHGs and co-operatives makes rural development participatory and self-sustaining.

sections.title: Rural Credit: Sources, Problems and KCC

blocks.text:
Rural credit is necessary for cultivation, purchase of inputs, investment and other rural activities. Credit can be classified according to duration and purpose.

Institutional sources include NABARD, commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks and Cooperative Credit Societies. These operate within the formal financial system. Non-institutional sources include moneylenders and other informal agencies. Informal credit may be easily available but can be costly.

Rural borrowers may face lack of collateral, delays, inadequate formal coverage and indebtedness. The Kisan Credit Card provides farmers a more convenient source of credit for agricultural and related needs. Expansion of accessible and affordable institutional credit is therefore important for rural development.

Need for rural credit: Farmers need money before the harvest for seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation and wages. They also need funds for buying cattle, machinery and land improvement, and sometimes for consumption during bad years. Since rural incomes are low and seasonal, credit fills the gap between expenditure and income.
Classification: Short-term (up to 15 months), medium-term (15 months to 5 years) and long-term (above 5 years) credit; productive and unproductive credit; secured and unsecured credit.

Institutional sources: (1) Co-operative credit societies and banks, the oldest formal source; (2) commercial banks, which expanded after nationalisation and priority-sector norms; (3) Regional Rural Banks serving small farmers, artisans and labourers; (4) NABARD, the apex body which refinances, supervises and plans rural credit. Non-institutional sources include moneylenders, landlords, traders and relatives, which are easily available but exploitative.

Problems and remedies: Lack of collateral, delays, complex procedures, inadequate coverage of small farmers, high overdues and continued dependence on moneylenders. The Kisan Credit Card (1998) offers a flexible revolving limit, low interest with subvention and insurance. Other remedies include SHG-bank linkage, microfinance, crop insurance (PMFBY), financial literacy and digital payment systems. Adequate institutional credit is thus a pillar of rural development.

sections.title: Models and Policies of Rural Development

blocks.text:
The Lewis model explains economic development through movement of labour from a traditional subsistence sector to a modern capitalist sector. Profits in the modern sector are reinvested, encouraging expansion and further employment.

The Gandhian model emphasizes village self-reliance, decentralization, local production, small and cottage industries and dignity of labour. It places the village at the centre of development.

Rural development policies are intended to improve employment, housing and livelihoods. MGNREGA provides guaranteed rural wage employment through public works. PMAY supports housing, while NRLM promotes livelihood opportunities through self-help groups and financial inclusion. These policies illustrate different dimensions of rural development.

Lewis model: The economy has a traditional (subsistence agricultural) sector with surplus labour and a modern (capitalist industrial) sector. Labour moves to the modern sector at a constant wage slightly above subsistence. Capitalists earn profits, reinvest them, and the modern sector expands, absorbing more labour. Growth continues until surplus labour is exhausted. Criticisms: reinvestment may be in labour-saving technology, wages may rise, agriculture may be neglected and urban unemployment may exist.

Gandhian model: Gandhi wanted self-reliant villages (Gram Swaraj) based on agriculture, khadi and village industries, decentralised power through panchayats, use of local resources, dignity of labour, trusteeship and simple living. It focuses on full employment and human values rather than only on output. It is criticised as idealistic but remains relevant for sustainable and inclusive development.

Policies: MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households, builds durable assets and gives women a large share of work. PMAY-G provides financial help for pucca houses with basic amenities. DAY-NRLM organises the rural poor into SHGs and federations and links them to banks and livelihood support. Other policies include PMGSY, Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen.

Conclusion: The Lewis model shows the importance of structural change, the Gandhian model emphasises village self-reliance, and modern policies combine employment, housing, livelihood and infrastructure to achieve inclusive rural development.
Adam Smith's classical approach associated economics with wealth and the causes of the wealth of nations. It emphasized production, accumulation and the material prosperity of society.

Adam Smith, called the 'Father of Economics', published 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' in 1776. He regarded economics as the science of wealth: how wealth is produced, increased and distributed. He stressed division of labour, free markets, self-interest guided by the 'invisible hand', and limited government interference.

Criticism: Critics such as Carlyle and Ruskin called it a 'dismal science' or 'bread-and-butter science' because it seemed to put wealth above human welfare. It also gave too narrow a meaning to wealth by focusing on material goods.
Marshall defined economics as a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, particularly those actions connected with the attainment and use of material requisites of well-being.

Marshall's definition appeared in 'Principles of Economics' (1890). It shifted the emphasis from wealth to human welfare: wealth is only a means to the end of welfare. Features include study of ordinary business of life, focus on material welfare, and economics as a social science concerned with people in society.

Criticism: Robbins argued that it is difficult to separate material and non-material welfare, that welfare cannot be measured, and that many economic activities (such as producing alcohol) may not promote welfare, yet they are studied by economics.

Robbins defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour as a relationship between unlimited ends and scarce means having alternative uses. Scarcity and choice are central to this definition.

Robbins gave this definition in 'An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science' (1932). It rests on three facts: human wants are unlimited, means (resources) are scarce, and these means have alternative uses. Hence people must choose, and economics becomes a science of choice.

Merits: It is universal, applies to all societies and makes economics a positive science. Criticism: It ignores welfare, treats economics as neutral between ends, does not cover problems of growth and unemployment of resources (as in a depression), and reduces economics to a mere valuation theory.
Economics studies how scarce resources are allocated among competing uses. Its scope includes consumption, production, exchange, distribution and the behaviour of individuals, firms and the economy.

Nature: Economics is both a science and an art. As a science it studies cause-and-effect relationships systematically; as a positive science it explains 'what is', and as a normative science it suggests 'what ought to be'. It is a social science because it studies human behaviour in society.

Scope: The subject matter includes consumption, production, exchange, distribution and public finance. It also covers micro and macro aspects, economic growth, international trade, money and banking, and the role of government. Economic laws are less exact than laws of natural sciences because human behaviour changes.
Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms and markets. Macroeconomics studies aggregates such as national income, employment, inflation and overall economic growth.

The terms were popularised by Ragnar Frisch. Microeconomics is also called price theory because it explains how prices of goods and factors are determined; it studies consumer behaviour, theory of the firm, market structures and factor pricing. Macroeconomics is called income and employment theory, developed especially by Keynes; it studies aggregate demand, aggregate supply, money, inflation, business cycles and growth.

Both are interdependent. Macro aggregates are built from individual decisions, and individual decisions are influenced by the macro environment, such as inflation or recession. A complete understanding of an economy needs both approaches.
Economic methodology includes the use of assumptions, models, logical reasoning and evidence to explain economic behaviour. Economics uses both deductive and inductive methods.

The deductive method (abstract or a priori) begins with general assumptions and derives conclusions by logic; it was used by classical economists like Ricardo. The inductive method (empirical or historical) starts from observed facts and statistics and arrives at generalisations; it was favoured by the German Historical School.

Modern economics uses both methods together. Economists build models with assumptions such as 'ceteris paribus' (other things being equal), derive hypotheses and then test them with data using statistics and econometrics.
Scarcity creates the basic problems of what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. Economies must make choices because resources have alternative uses.

What to produce: which goods and in what quantities, for example food grains or luxury goods, consumer goods or capital goods. How to produce: the choice of technique, whether labour-intensive or capital-intensive. For whom to produce: how the output is distributed among people, which depends on income distribution.

Other basic problems include whether resources are fully utilised (problem of unemployment), how efficiently they are used, and how the economy can grow over time. Capitalist economies solve these problems through the price mechanism, socialist economies through central planning and mixed economies like India through a combination of both.
The price mechanism is the process through which demand and supply determine prices and help allocate resources in a market economy.

In a free market, prices act as signals. When demand for a good rises, its price rises, which encourages producers to supply more and attracts resources to that industry. When demand falls, price falls and resources move elsewhere. In this way prices solve the problems of what, how and for whom to produce without central direction, as described by Adam Smith's 'invisible hand'.
Limitations: The price mechanism may lead to inequality, neglect of public goods, monopolies, externalities such as pollution and instability. Hence governments intervene in mixed economies.
Demand is the quantity of a commodity consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices during a given period, other things remaining constant.

Demand is different from mere desire or want. A want becomes demand only when it is backed by willingness and ability to pay. Demand always refers to a particular price and a particular period of time.

Demand can be shown through a demand schedule (a table of prices and quantities) and a demand curve (a graph sloping downward from left to right). Types of demand include individual and market demand, price, income and cross demand, joint demand, composite demand and derived demand.
The law of demand states that, other things remaining constant, quantity demanded generally rises when price falls and falls when price rises.

Reasons for the law: (1) law of diminishing marginal utility; (2) income effect - a fall in price increases real income; (3) substitution effect - the good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes; (4) new buyers enter the market; (5) multiple uses of some goods.

Exceptions: Giffen goods (inferior staples consumed by the poor), Veblen or prestige goods, expectations of further price changes, ignorance of quality, and necessities. Assumptions of the law include constant income, tastes, prices of related goods and no expectation of future price change.
Demand is influenced by the commodity's price, consumer income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations and the number of buyers.

Explanation: Normally a rise in income increases demand for normal goods but may reduce demand for inferior goods. A rise in the price of a substitute (e.g. tea) raises demand for coffee, while a rise in the price of a complement (e.g. petrol) reduces demand for cars. Favourable tastes and advertising increase demand.

Other factors include distribution of income, population size and composition, climate and season, government policy (taxes and subsidies), availability of credit and expectations about future prices and income. The demand function is written as Dx = f(Px, Y, Pr, T, E, N).
Supply is the quantity of a commodity producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices during a given period.

Supply differs from stock. Stock is the total quantity available with sellers, while supply is the part of the stock that is actually offered for sale at a given price. Supply is shown by a supply schedule and an upward-sloping supply curve.

Determinants of supply include the price of the good, prices of factors of production, technology, prices of related goods, goals of the firm, number of firms, taxes and subsidies, natural factors and expectations of future prices.
Other things remaining constant, quantity supplied generally increases as price rises and decreases as price falls.

Reasons: a higher price increases profit, encouraging existing firms to produce more and new firms to enter; higher marginal cost at larger output requires higher prices. The supply curve therefore slopes upward from left to right.

Exceptions include the backward-bending supply curve of labour (beyond a high wage workers prefer leisure), agricultural goods whose supply is fixed in the short run, perishable goods, and expectations of a future fall in price, which may increase present supply.
A movement along a demand curve results from a change in the commodity's own price. A shift of the entire curve results from changes in other determinants such as income or tastes.
Movement along the curve is called extension (more quantity demanded when price falls) or contraction (less demanded when price rises). It involves moving from one point to another on the same curve.

A shift of the curve is called increase (rightward shift, more demanded at every price) or decrease (leftward shift). For example, a rise in income shifts the demand curve for a normal good to the right, while a fall in the price of a substitute shifts it to the left.
A movement along a supply curve results from a change in own price, while a shift occurs because of changes in technology, input prices, taxes or other non-price determinants.

Movement along the supply curve is called extension (more supplied at a higher price) or contraction (less supplied at a lower price). It occurs only because of change in the price of the commodity itself.

A rightward shift (increase in supply) may occur due to better technology, lower input costs or subsidies; a leftward shift (decrease in supply) may occur because of higher input costs, new taxes or natural calamities such as floods that damage crops.

Elasticity measures responsiveness of demand to changes in economic variables. Price elasticity measures response to price, income elasticity to income, and cross elasticity to the price of another good.

Price elasticity (Ep) = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. Demand may be perfectly elastic (infinite), relatively elastic (greater than 1), unitary elastic (equal to 1), relatively inelastic (less than 1) or perfectly inelastic (zero).

Methods of measurement include the percentage method, total outlay (expenditure) method, point method and arc method. Factors affecting elasticity: nature of the good (necessity or luxury), availability of substitutes, proportion of income spent, number of uses, time period and habits. Elasticity is useful for pricing, taxation, international trade and wage policy.
The cardinal approach assumes utility can be measured numerically. Consumer choice is explained through total and marginal utility.

This approach was developed by Jevons, Menger, Walras and especially Marshall. Utility is measured in imaginary units called 'utils', and money is used as a measuring rod. Total utility is the sum of utility from all units consumed, and marginal utility is the addition to total utility from one more unit.

Assumptions: rational consumer, constant marginal utility of money, independent utilities and homogeneous units. Criticism: utility is subjective and cannot be measured exactly, and marginal utility of money is not constant. These criticisms led to the ordinal approach.
The ordinal approach assumes consumers can rank combinations of goods according to preference without measuring utility in exact units.

The ordinal approach was developed by Hicks and Allen (1934) using indifference curves. The consumer only needs to say whether one bundle is preferred to, less preferred than, or equally preferred to another. Utility numbers such as first, second, third show ranks only.

Assumptions include rationality, consistency and transitivity of choice, non-satiety (more is preferred to less) and diminishing marginal rate of substitution. It is considered more realistic than the cardinal approach.
The law states that as a consumer consumes successive units of a commodity, the additional utility from each extra unit tends to decline, other things remaining constant.

Example: A thirsty person gets great satisfaction from the first glass of water, less from the second and still less from the third; eventually marginal utility may become zero or negative. Total utility increases at a diminishing rate, becomes maximum when marginal utility is zero, and falls when marginal utility is negative.

Assumptions: homogeneous units, continuous consumption, reasonable size of units, no change in taste, income or fashion. Exceptions: hobbies, money, music, rare goods. Importance: basis of the law of demand, progressive taxation, consumer surplus and the diamond-water paradox.
A consumer maximizes satisfaction by allocating expenditure so that marginal utility per unit of money is equal across goods, subject to income and prices.

This law is also called the law of substitution or Gossen's second law. Equilibrium condition: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = ... = MUm (marginal utility of money). If the marginal utility per rupee of one good is higher, the consumer gains by spending more on it and less on the other.

Limitations: consumers may not be fully rational, utility cannot be measured, goods may be indivisible and habits or fashion influence spending. Uses: it applies to consumption, production, exchange, distribution and public finance (allocation of government expenditure).
The paradox contrasts the high usefulness but low market price of water with the lower total usefulness but high price of diamonds. Marginal utility and scarcity help explain the difference.

Adam Smith observed that water has great 'value in use' but little 'value in exchange', while diamonds have little value in use but great value in exchange. The classical economists could not explain this properly.

The marginal utility approach solves it: water is abundant, so the marginal utility of the last unit is very low, and price depends on marginal utility, not total utility. Diamonds are scarce, so their marginal utility and price are high, even though the total utility of water is far greater.
An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods giving a consumer the same level of satisfaction. It normally slopes downward and is convex to the origin.

Properties: (1) slopes downward from left to right, because to get more of one good the consumer must give up some of the other; (2) convex to the origin, because of diminishing marginal rate of substitution (MRS); (3) two indifference curves never intersect; (4) a higher curve represents a higher level of satisfaction.

A set of indifference curves is called an indifference map. The slope of an indifference curve is the MRS of X for Y, which shows how much of Y the consumer is willing to sacrifice for one more unit of X.
A budget line shows all combinations of two goods that a consumer can purchase with a given income at given prices.
If income is M and prices are Px and Py, the budget equation is Px.X + Py.Y = M. The line meets the X-axis at M/Px and the Y-axis at M/Py. Its slope equals the price ratio Px/Py.

Changes: an increase in income shifts the line parallel outward; a decrease shifts it inward. A change in the price of one good rotates the line around the axis of the other good. Points on the line are attainable with full expenditure, points inside are attainable but leave money unspent, and points outside are unattainable.
Under indifference-curve analysis, equilibrium occurs where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, subject to the required conditions.

Conditions: (1) the necessary condition is that the budget line is tangent to the indifference curve, so MRSxy = Px/Py; (2) the sufficient condition is that the indifference curve is convex to the origin at the point of equilibrium.

At this point the consumer gets maximum satisfaction from given income and prices. Any other point on the budget line lies on a lower indifference curve, while higher curves are out of reach. Changes in income and prices give the income-consumption and price-consumption curves.
A price change affects consumption through substitution and income effects. Hicks and Slutsky provide different methods of decomposing the total price effect.

Price effect = substitution effect + income effect. Hicks's method removes the income effect by compensating variation in income so that the consumer stays on the original indifference curve; the movement along that curve is the substitution effect. Slutsky's method adjusts income so that the consumer can just buy the original bundle (cost-difference method).

The substitution effect is always negative (the consumer buys more of the cheaper good). The income effect is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods. In Giffen goods, the negative income effect is stronger than the substitution effect, so demand falls when price falls.
An Engel curve shows the relationship between consumer income and quantity demanded of a commodity, other relevant factors remaining constant.

The Engel curve is named after Ernst Engel, the German statistician. It is derived from the income-consumption curve. For normal goods it slopes upward; for inferior goods it slopes backward (negative) after a certain income level.

Engel's Law states that as family income increases, the proportion of income spent on food declines, even though total food expenditure may rise. Engel curves are useful for forecasting demand and studying household budgets.
Consumer surplus is the difference between the maximum amount a consumer is willing to pay and the amount actually paid.

The concept was developed by Dupuit and popularised by Marshall. Consumer surplus = what the consumer is willing to pay - what the consumer actually pays. Graphically, it is the area below the demand curve and above the market price line.

Example: If a person is ready to pay Rs 50 for a book but buys it for Rs 30, the consumer surplus is Rs 20. Uses: in taxation policy, monopoly pricing, comparing living conditions, public projects and international trade. Criticism: it is hypothetical, assumes measurable utility and is difficult to measure for necessities.
A production function expresses the technical relationship between quantities of inputs and the maximum output that can be produced.

It can be written as Q = f(L, K, Land, Organisation), where Q is output and L and K are labour and capital. It shows the maximum output obtainable from given inputs with a given technology. A change in technology shifts the production function.

There are two types: the short-run production function, in which some inputs are fixed (studied through the law of variable proportions), and the long-run production function, in which all inputs are variable (studied through returns to scale). The Cobb-Douglas production function Q = A L^a K^b is a well-known example.
An isoquant shows different combinations of inputs that produce the same level of output. Isoquants normally slope downward and are convex to the origin.

The word 'iso' means equal and 'quant' means quantity. Isoquants are also called equal-product or iso-product curves. Properties: they slope downward, are convex due to diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS), do not intersect, and higher isoquants show higher output.

Unlike indifference curves, isoquants can be labelled with exact output quantities (e.g. 100 units). The slope of the isoquant is MRTS of labour for capital, i.e. the amount of capital that can be replaced by one unit of labour keeping output constant.
An iso-cost line shows combinations of inputs that can be purchased for a given total cost at given input prices.

It is also called the equal-cost line or budget line of the producer. If total cost is C and the prices of labour and capital are w and r, then wL + rK = C. Its slope is w/r, the ratio of factor prices.

An increase in total outlay shifts the iso-cost line outward in parallel, and a change in one factor price changes its slope. Together with the isoquant map it determines the least-cost combination of factors.
A producer reaches equilibrium when a given output is produced at minimum cost or maximum output is obtained for a given cost, commonly at tangency between an isoquant and iso-cost line.
Conditions: (1) the iso-cost line must be tangent to the isoquant, meaning MRTSLK = w/r (equivalently MPL/w = MPK/r); (2) the isoquant must be convex to the origin at that point.

This is called the least-cost combination of factors. If the producer moves away from this point, either the cost increases for the same output or the output falls for the same cost. As the outlay changes, the series of equilibrium points forms the expansion path.
This law explains changes in output when one input varies while other inputs remain fixed in the short run. Marginal product eventually tends to decline.

The law has three stages: Stage I - increasing returns, where total product rises at an increasing rate and marginal product rises; Stage II - diminishing returns, where total product rises at a diminishing rate and marginal product falls but remains positive; Stage III - negative returns, where total product falls and marginal product is negative.

A rational producer operates in Stage II. Causes of diminishing returns include fixity of some factors, imperfect substitutability of factors and over-use of the fixed factor. Assumptions: constant technology, homogeneous units of the variable factor and short-run period.
Returns to scale examine how output changes when all inputs are changed proportionately in the long run. Returns may be increasing, constant or decreasing.

Increasing returns to scale occur when output increases more than proportionately to inputs (doubling inputs more than doubles output), usually due to division of labour and specialisation. Constant returns occur when output increases in the same proportion. Decreasing returns occur when output increases less than proportionately, often because of management difficulties.
The difference from the law of variable proportions is that returns to scale apply to the long run, when all factors are variable and the scale of the firm changes.
Economies of scale reduce average cost as output expands, while diseconomies cause average cost to rise beyond a certain scale.

Internal economies arise within a firm as it grows: technical economies (better machines), managerial economies (specialised managers), marketing economies (bulk buying and selling), financial economies (cheaper loans) and risk-bearing economies. External economies arise from growth of the whole industry, such as better transport, skilled labour pools and information.

Diseconomies include difficulties of management and coordination, labour problems, rising input prices, and external diseconomies such as congestion and pollution. These explain why the long-run average cost curve is U-shaped.
The expansion path joins cost-minimizing input combinations for different levels of output, given input prices.

When the producer's outlay increases with constant factor prices, the iso-cost line shifts outward, and new tangency points with higher isoquants are reached. The locus of these points is the expansion path.

If the production function is homogeneous, the expansion path is a straight line from the origin. The expansion path shows how a firm should expand its use of inputs as it grows, and it links production theory with cost theory.
Important cost concepts include fixed cost, variable cost, total cost, average cost and marginal cost. Their relationships help explain production decisions.

Fixed costs (rent, interest, salaries of permanent staff) do not change with output in the short run, while variable costs (raw materials, power, wages of casual labour) change with output. TC = TFC + TVC. Average cost AC = TC/Q, and marginal cost MC = change in TC due to one extra unit.

AFC falls continuously as output rises; AVC, AC and MC are U-shaped because of the law of variable proportions. MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points. Other concepts include opportunity cost, explicit and implicit costs, private and social costs, and long-run average cost (envelope curve).
Producer surplus is the difference between the amount producers receive and the minimum amount they would be willing to accept for supplying a good.

It is measured as the area above the supply curve and below the market price. For example, if a farmer is ready to sell rice at Rs 25 per kg but the market price is Rs 35, the producer surplus is Rs 10 per kg.
Producer surplus together with consumer surplus forms total economic surplus, which is used to measure the welfare effects of market changes, taxes, subsidies and trade policies.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative sacrificed when a choice is made.

It is also called alternative cost or transfer earnings. Example: if a farmer can grow either wheat or sugarcane on a piece of land, and chooses wheat, the opportunity cost of wheat is the sugarcane that could have been grown. Similarly, a student's opportunity cost of attending college includes the wages given up.

Opportunity cost explains the need for choice due to scarcity, the production possibility curve, factor pricing (transfer earnings and rent), and rational decision-making by consumers, firms and governments.

sections.title: Definitions, Nature, Scope and Basic Economic Problems

blocks.text:
Economics has been defined differently by major economists. Adam Smith emphasized wealth, Alfred Marshall connected economics with material welfare, and Lionel Robbins emphasized scarcity, choice and alternative uses of resources.

Economics studies production, consumption, exchange, distribution and allocation of scarce resources. Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms and markets, whereas macroeconomics studies aggregates such as national income and employment.

The fundamental economic problem is scarcity. Because resources are limited and wants are many, every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. The price mechanism is one method through which market demand and supply guide these decisions.

Definitions in detail: (1) Wealth definition - Adam Smith (1776) treated economics as the science of wealth; it was criticised for being materialistic and narrow. (2) Welfare definition - Marshall (1890) said economics studies mankind in the ordinary business of life, emphasising material welfare; it was criticised because welfare is vague and unmeasurable. (3) Scarcity definition - Robbins (1932) said economics studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses; it is universal but neutral about ends. (4) Growth-oriented definition - Samuelson included economic growth and the use of resources over time.
Nature: Economics is a social science, both positive and normative, and both a science and an art. Its laws are statements of tendencies and are less exact than physical laws.

Scope: It covers consumption, production, exchange, distribution and public finance; microeconomics deals with individual units and price determination, while macroeconomics deals with aggregates, income, employment, money and growth. Methods include deductive and inductive reasoning.

Basic problems: What to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce, plus full employment and growth. The production possibility curve illustrates scarcity and opportunity cost. In a market economy the price mechanism solves these problems; in a planned economy the state does so; in a mixed economy such as India both play a role.

Demand is the quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at different prices. The law of demand describes an inverse relation between price and quantity demanded, other things remaining constant. Supply refers to quantities producers are willing and able to sell, and the law of supply generally describes a direct relation with price.

A change in own price causes movement along a demand or supply curve, while changes in non-price determinants shift the curve. Market demand is obtained by combining individual demands.

Elasticity measures responsiveness. Price elasticity measures the response of demand to price, income elasticity to income, and cross elasticity to the price of another commodity. Elasticity is important for pricing and understanding consumer response.

Demand and its law: Demand means desire backed by ability and willingness to pay. The law of demand is explained by diminishing marginal utility, income and substitution effects and new consumers. Exceptions include Giffen goods, Veblen goods and speculative demand. Determinants include price, income, prices of related goods, tastes, population, expectations and government policy.

Supply and its law: Supply is the quantity offered for sale at a given price and time. It rises with price because of profit motive and rising marginal cost. Determinants include input prices, technology, number of firms, taxes and natural factors.

Movement versus shift: Extension and contraction refer to movement along the same curve due to change in own price; increase and decrease refer to shifts due to other factors. Market equilibrium occurs where demand equals supply.

Elasticity: Price elasticity has five degrees from perfectly elastic to perfectly inelastic, measured by percentage, total outlay, point and arc methods. Income elasticity is positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods; cross elasticity is positive for substitutes and negative for complements. Elasticity guides business pricing, government taxation (taxing inelastic goods raises more revenue), wage bargaining and international trade policy.

Consumer theory explains how consumers allocate limited income among goods. The cardinal approach treats utility as measurable, while the ordinal approach ranks preferences. The law of diminishing marginal utility states that additional satisfaction tends to fall with successive consumption. Equi-marginal utility explains allocation of expenditure across goods.

Indifference-curve analysis uses curves showing equally preferred combinations. A budget line represents purchasing possibilities. Consumer equilibrium occurs at the highest attainable indifference curve, normally where it is tangent to the budget line.

A change in price creates income and substitution effects, decomposed by Hicks and Slutsky. Engel curves relate demand to income. Consumer surplus measures the excess of willingness to pay over actual payment.

Cardinal analysis: Marshall's approach assumes utility can be measured in utils and that marginal utility of money is constant. The law of diminishing marginal utility and the law of equi-marginal utility (MUx/Px = MUy/Py) explain consumer equilibrium and the downward slope of the demand curve. Weaknesses: utility is subjective and the constant marginal utility of money is unrealistic.

Ordinal analysis: Hicks and Allen used indifference curves, which slope downward, are convex, never intersect and show higher satisfaction when higher. The budget line Px.X + Py.Y = M shows attainable combinations. Equilibrium is where MRSxy = Px/Py with convexity.

Price, income and substitution effects: A fall in price increases real income (income effect) and makes the good relatively cheaper (substitution effect). Hicks uses compensating variation; Slutsky uses the cost-difference method. For Giffen goods the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

Engel curve and consumer surplus: The Engel curve shows how demand changes with income; Engel's law says the share of food falls as income rises. Consumer surplus, the difference between willingness to pay and actual payment, measures the benefit consumers receive from the market and is useful in taxation and public policy.

A production function describes the technical relationship between inputs and output. Isoquants show input combinations producing equal output, while iso-cost lines show combinations available at equal cost. Producer equilibrium occurs at the appropriate tangency of these curves.

The law of variable proportions applies when one input changes while others are fixed. Returns to scale concern proportional changes in all inputs. Economies of scale reduce average cost as production expands, while diseconomies raise it after a certain point.

The expansion path traces optimal input combinations as output changes. Cost analysis uses fixed, variable, total, average and marginal costs. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative sacrificed, while producer surplus measures the excess of actual receipts over the minimum acceptable amount.

Production function: Q = f(L, K) shows the technical relationship between inputs and maximum output. In the short run, the law of variable proportions applies with three stages - increasing, diminishing and negative returns - and producers operate in the second stage. In the long run, returns to scale may be increasing, constant or decreasing.

Producer equilibrium: Isoquants (downward sloping, convex, non-intersecting) and the iso-cost line (wL + rK = C) together determine the least-cost combination, where MRTS = w/r. Joining equilibrium points at different cost levels gives the expansion path.

Economies of scale: Internal economies (technical, managerial, marketing, financial, risk-bearing) and external economies (infrastructure, skilled labour, information) reduce cost; diseconomies arise from management problems and congestion.

Costs: Short-run costs include TFC, TVC, TC, AFC, AVC, AC and MC. AVC, AC and MC are U-shaped and MC cuts AC at its minimum. Long-run AC is an envelope of short-run AC curves. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative foregone, explicit costs are actual payments and implicit costs are the value of owned resources. Producer surplus is the gain to sellers above their minimum acceptable price.
Adam Smith emphasized wealth in economics, while Lionel Robbins emphasized scarcity, choice and alternative uses of limited means.
Scarcity creates the problems of what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.
Demand concerns quantities buyers are willing and able to buy; supply concerns quantities sellers are willing and able to sell. Their interaction helps determine market price.
National income measures the value of income or output generated by an economy during a period. Measurement requires avoiding double counting and accounting for relevant components.
A government budget is an annual statement of estimated public receipts and expenditure. Budgets may be balanced, surplus or deficit.
The budget is prepared by the government and placed before Parliament for authorization through the constitutional legislative process.
Public revenue is income received by government from tax and non-tax sources.
Public expenditure is spending by government on administration, development, welfare, infrastructure and other public purposes.
The Indian economy is a large mixed developing economy with agriculture, industry and services, significant regional diversity and continuing challenges of employment, poverty and inequality.
Population analysis includes size, growth rate and sex ratio, all of which influence economic planning and development.
Economic growth refers mainly to sustained increase in real output or income, while economic development is broader and includes structural and qualitative improvement in living conditions.

Economic reforms refer to policy changes intended to improve economic efficiency and performance. In India, major reforms from 1991 are associated with liberalization, privatization and globalization.

Economics deals with scarcity and choice. Smith's definition emphasized wealth, while Robbins emphasized unlimited ends and scarce means with alternative uses. Scarcity requires every economy to decide what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

Demand and supply are basic market concepts. The law of demand generally states that quantity demanded falls when price rises, other things constant, while the law of supply generally states that quantity supplied rises with price. Their interaction helps determine market outcomes.

National income measures economic activity and can be approached through output, income and expenditure. A government budget is an annual statement of expected receipts and expenditure and may be balanced, surplus or deficit.

In India the budget is prepared by the government and requires legislative approval. Public revenue comes from tax and non-tax sources, while public expenditure finances administration, development, welfare and public services.

sections.title: Indian Economy, Population, Growth and Reforms

blocks.text:
The Indian economy contains agriculture, industry and services and is characterized by considerable regional and social diversity. Population size, growth and sex ratio are important demographic indicators.

Economic growth mainly means sustained increase in real output, while economic development includes broader structural and social improvement. Economic reforms in India, particularly from 1991, are associated with liberalization, privatization and globalization.

Banking in India developed from early indigenous and presidency banking to a modern regulated system. Major changes include expansion of commercial banking, establishment of the RBI and growth of specialized and development financial institutions.
A central bank is the apex monetary institution of a country. It regulates money and credit, manages currency and supports stability of the financial system.
Major functions include issue of currency, banker to government, bankers' bank, lender of last resort, management of reserves and control of credit.
Quantitative methods influence the overall volume of credit. They include policy rates, reserve requirements and open-market operations.
Qualitative methods regulate the direction or use of credit through selective measures rather than only changing total credit.
The Reserve Bank of India is India's central bank. It regulates the banking system, conducts monetary policy, manages currency and performs developmental and supervisory functions.
Monetary policy refers to central-bank measures influencing money supply, credit and interest conditions to pursue objectives such as price stability, growth and financial stability.
Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange and means of payment. It also serves as a unit of account and store of value.
Money performs primary functions as medium of exchange and measure of value, and other functions such as store of value and standard of deferred payments.
Money may take different forms, including metallic, paper, bank or deposit money and modern digital forms.
Commercial banks accept deposits, provide loans, facilitate payments and offer other financial services to households and businesses.
Commercial banks create deposit credit through lending, subject to reserves, regulations and demand for loans.
Savings deposits encourage personal saving; current deposits support frequent transactions; fixed deposits are kept for a fixed period; recurring deposits involve regular periodic saving.
A cheque is a written instruction by an account holder directing a bank to pay a specified sum according to its terms.
A pass book is a record of transactions in a customer's bank account, traditionally maintained by the bank for the account holder.
A demand draft is a bank-issued payment instrument directing payment of a specified amount to a named person or entity.
A debit card uses funds from the holder's bank account, while a credit card allows purchases against an approved credit facility.
Internet and mobile banking allow customers to access accounts and perform banking transactions electronically.
Digital currency is money represented and transferred in digital form. The syllabus introduces the concept within modern banking services.
Co-operative banks are financial institutions organized on cooperative principles to serve members and communities, including agricultural and rural borrowers.
Development banks provide medium- and long-term financial support for development-oriented sectors and projects.
SIDBI is a development financial institution focused on promotion, financing and development of micro, small and medium enterprises.
IDBI historically developed as an important development financial institution supporting industrial finance; its institutional form has changed over time.
Export-Import Bank of India supports and finances India's international trade and related activities.
NABARD is the apex development institution concerned with agriculture and rural development finance.
National Housing Bank is an apex institution associated with housing finance and development of the housing-finance system.
A financial market facilitates transfer of funds and trading of financial assets. Its major segments include the money market and capital market.
The money market deals mainly in short-term funds and financial instruments.
The capital market deals mainly with medium- and long-term funds and securities. It includes primary and secondary markets.
The primary market deals with new issues of securities, while the secondary market enables trading of securities already issued.
The syllabus includes call money, Treasury Bills, commercial papers, commercial bills and trade bills as money-market instruments.
Capital-market instruments in the syllabus include debentures, shares, bonds and equity.
The stock market provides a platform for buying and selling securities and contributes to liquidity, price discovery and mobilization of investment funds.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India regulates the securities market and works to protect investors and promote orderly development of the market.
The Eurodollar market refers to deposits and transactions in US dollars held outside the United States.

sections.title: Indian Banking System, RBI and Monetary Policy

blocks.text:
India's banking system has evolved into a regulated network of commercial, cooperative and specialized institutions. At its apex is the Reserve Bank of India, which performs central-banking functions.

A central bank issues currency, acts as banker to government and banks, manages reserves and regulates credit. Quantitative credit-control measures influence the overall amount of credit, while qualitative methods influence its direction or use.

Monetary policy is the use of monetary and credit instruments to influence economic conditions. Its objectives include price stability, growth and financial stability. The RBI therefore performs both regulatory and developmental roles in India's financial system.

Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard for deferred payments. It can take metallic, paper, deposit and digital forms.

Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and provide payment services. Through lending they participate in credit creation, subject to reserves and regulation. Major deposits include savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits.

Modern banking uses cheques, pass books, demand drafts, debit and credit cards, internet banking and mobile banking. The syllabus also introduces digital currency, reflecting the growing role of electronic forms of money and payment.

Co-operative banks are organized on cooperative principles and serve members and communities, including rural borrowers. Development banks provide specialized finance for sectors important to economic development.

The syllabus identifies SIDBI for the MSME sector, IDBI in industrial development finance, EXIM Bank for international trade, NABARD for agriculture and rural development, and National Housing Bank for the housing-finance system.

These institutions complement ordinary commercial banking by directing financial support toward sectors requiring specialized or long-term development finance.

Financial markets channel savings toward investment and permit trading of financial assets. The money market mainly handles short-term funds, while the capital market handles medium- and long-term finance.

The primary market issues new securities and the secondary market trades existing ones. Money-market instruments include call money, Treasury Bills, commercial paper and commercial or trade bills. Capital-market instruments include shares, debentures, bonds and equity securities.

Stock exchanges provide liquidity and price discovery. SEBI regulates India's securities market and protects investors. The Eurodollar market refers to US-dollar deposits and transactions outside the United States.
A market is an arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods, services or factors of production.
Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the prevailing price.
Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products and strong competitive conditions. Imperfect markets depart from one or more of these conditions.
Perfect competition is characterized by many firms, homogeneous products, free entry and exit and firms acting as price takers. Firm equilibrium is studied in short-run and long-run conditions.
Monopoly is a market with a single seller and strong barriers to entry. The monopolist faces the market demand curve and chooses output and price subject to demand and cost conditions.
The shutdown point is the short-run condition below which a competitive firm cannot cover its variable costs and therefore stops production.
Zero economic profit means total revenue covers all explicit and implicit costs, including normal return. It does not mean the firm receives no accounting income.
Price discrimination occurs when a seller charges different prices for the same product to different buyers or markets when differences are not simply due to cost.
Price discrimination is commonly classified into first, second and third degree according to how prices vary across units or groups of buyers.
Controlled prices are influenced or fixed by public authority, while administered prices are set by producers or institutions rather than determined purely by immediate market forces.
Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering differentiated products. Firms have some price-setting power but face competition from close substitutes.
Oligopoly is a market dominated by a small number of firms whose decisions are interdependent.
The kinked demand curve model explains price rigidity in oligopoly by assuming rivals respond differently to price increases and price cuts.
Duopoly is a special form of oligopoly with two major sellers whose decisions affect one another.
Monopsony is a market situation with a single major buyer.
Bilateral monopoly exists when a single seller faces a single buyer, making price and quantity dependent on bargaining power.
The marginal productivity theory relates factor rewards to the additional contribution made by a unit of the factor to production, subject to its assumptions.
Wage theories explain the determination of the price of labour. In market analysis, wages are influenced by demand for and supply of labour along with institutional factors.
Scarcity rent arises when the supply of a factor or resource is fixed or scarce relative to demand.
Differential rent arises because units of land or resources differ in fertility, productivity or location.
Quasi-rent is a temporary surplus earned by certain man-made factors whose supply is fixed in the short run.
The classical theory explains interest through the interaction of saving and investment.
Keynes explained interest mainly through liquidity preference and the supply of money.
The innovation theory associates profit with successful entrepreneurial innovation.

sections.title: Risk and Uncertainty Theories of Profit

blocks.text: These theories associate profit with bearing business risk or uncertainty that cannot be fully predicted or insured.
A factor market is a market in which services of productive factors such as labour and capital are bought and sold.
Factor-market equilibrium occurs where demand for a factor and its supply are balanced under the relevant market conditions.
Welfare economics studies how allocation of resources affects social well-being and evaluates economic arrangements using specified welfare criteria.
Classical welfare analysis sought to relate economic policies and resource allocation to social welfare, often using utility and distributional considerations.
A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. A Pareto-optimal allocation is one where no further Pareto improvement is possible.
A value judgment is a normative assessment about what is desirable or fair. Welfare economics often requires awareness of where such judgments enter analysis.
The Kaldor-Hicks principle treats a change as potentially welfare-improving if gainers could compensate losers and still remain better off, even if compensation is not actually paid.
A social welfare function represents social welfare as depending on the welfare or utilities of individuals according to specified social judgments.

Market equilibrium occurs where demand and supply are balanced. Perfect competition is characterized by many firms, homogeneous products, free entry and exit and price-taking behaviour. A competitive firm's short-run and long-run equilibrium depends on revenue and cost conditions. The shutdown point concerns inability to cover variable cost in the short run, while zero economic profit means all economic costs are covered.

Monopoly has a single seller protected by barriers to entry. The monopolist has greater control over price but remains constrained by demand. Price discrimination occurs when different prices are charged to different buyers or units under appropriate conditions. Controlled and administered prices show that not all prices are determined by unrestricted market competition.

sections.title: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly and Other Imperfect Markets

blocks.text:
Monopolistic competition combines many sellers with product differentiation. Each firm has some control over price but competes with close substitutes. Short-run and long-run equilibrium reflects this combination of differentiation and entry.

Oligopoly contains a few interdependent firms. The kinked-demand model explains why prices may remain rigid when firms expect asymmetric responses from rivals. Duopoly is an oligopoly with two sellers.

Monopsony describes a market with a single buyer, while bilateral monopoly places a single buyer against a single seller. These structures show how market power may arise on either the selling or buying side.

Factor pricing explains rewards to factors of production. The marginal productivity theory relates factor payment to marginal contribution to output under its assumptions. Wage determination concerns the price of labour.

Rent may take several forms. Scarcity rent results from restricted supply, differential rent from differences in productivity or location, and quasi-rent is a temporary surplus on certain man-made factors in the short run.

The classical theory of interest emphasizes saving and investment, while Keynesian theory emphasizes liquidity preference and money supply. Profit theories include innovation, risk and uncertainty. Factor-market equilibrium occurs where factor demand and supply are balanced under relevant market conditions.

Welfare economics evaluates how economic arrangements affect social well-being. Classical welfare economics provided early methods of linking allocation with welfare.

The Pareto criterion calls a change an improvement when at least one person becomes better off and nobody becomes worse off. A Pareto optimum is reached when no such improvement remains possible. The criterion is limited because many real policy changes create both gainers and losers.

The Kaldor-Hicks compensation principle asks whether gainers could potentially compensate losers and still gain. Welfare analysis also involves value judgments about desirable outcomes. A social welfare function provides a formal way of relating individual welfare to an overall social evaluation.
The syllabus repeats the basic definitions of Adam Smith and Lionel Robbins, basic economic problems, and the concept and laws of demand and supply.
The syllabus covers national income in India, meaning and kinds of budget, budget preparation and passing procedure, public revenue and public expenditure.
The syllabus covers characteristics of the Indian economy, population size, growth rate and sex ratio, economic growth and development, and economic reforms.

Adam Smith emphasized wealth, while Lionel Robbins emphasized scarcity and choice. Scarcity creates the problems of what, how and for whom to produce. Demand and supply describe buyer and seller behaviour and help explain market price.

National income measures aggregate economic activity. Government budgets state expected receipts and expenditure and may be balanced, surplus or deficit. Public revenue finances government, while public expenditure is incurred for administration, development and public services.

The Indian economy includes agriculture, industry and services and faces continuing development challenges. Population indicators include size, growth and sex ratio. Growth refers mainly to increasing real output, while development includes wider structural and welfare improvements. Economic reforms are associated especially with policy changes introduced from 1991.
